name: XBRL Tagging and Regulatory Filing
title: XBRL Tagging and Regulatory Filing
answer: XBRL tagging and regulatory filing covers the preparation of machine-readable financial statements and disclosures for submission to regulators. It includes mapping financial line items to a standard taxonomy, creating instance documents, and validating the resulting data against filing rules. The work spans both quantitative facts, such as revenue or assets, and narrative disclosures through inline XBRL. It sits within financial reporting and synthesis, where the goal is to make reported data comparable and automatically processable.

sections.body: XBRL tagging and regulatory filing covers the preparation of machine-readable financial statements and disclosures for submission to regulators. It includes mapping financial line items to a standard taxonomy, creating instance documents, and validating the resulting data against filing rules. The work spans both quantitative facts, such as revenue or assets, and narrative disclosures through inline XBRL. It sits within financial reporting and synthesis, where the goal is to make reported data comparable and automatically processable.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The process runs on XBRL taxonomies published by regulators, filing software that generates instance documents, and validation engines that check calculations and consistency. Data typically flows from an ERP or consolidation system into a tagging tool, then into the regulator's electronic filing system. AI components may run on cloud infrastructure and use natural language processing models to suggest tags for text blocks or to extract figures from PDFs. The infrastructure must maintain a clear link between each tagged fact and its source in the financial statements.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a review of the financial statements to identify reportable facts and their appropriate taxonomy concepts. Taggers then assign elements, create contexts for periods and dimensions, and build the instance document. AI can assist by recommending tags based on prior filings, flagging inconsistencies between similar disclosures, and checking that calculations foot and cross-foot. Human reviewers reconcile the tagged data to the source documents and resolve validation errors before submission. The process is iterative, often requiring several rounds of correction before the filing is accepted.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in XBRL filing center on data provenance, audit trails, and the accuracy of the tagged data. Each tag should be traceable to a source document, and firms typically maintain version control over taxonomy extensions and filing drafts. Mis-tagging can lead to regulatory comment letters, restatements, or enforcement action, so controls and qualified review are standard practice. The public nature of many filings means that once submitted, the tagged data is available for automated analysis by investors, researchers, and competitors. Provenance of any AI model used in tagging also matters, particularly if the model was trained on proprietary or licensed data.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more automated tagging, with AI models increasingly used to map disclosures to taxonomies and to detect anomalies before filing. Regulators continue to expand structured data requirements, and inline XBRL is becoming the norm for narrative sections as well as financial statements. Real-time or event-driven filing may reduce the lag between a corporate action and its public disclosure. Over time, the boundary between the filing process and continuous internal reporting is likely to blur, as the same tagged data serves both regulatory and management purposes.
